newsitem.title: CANADA: Wanted Saudi reportedly admitted Hizbollah ties.
newsitem.headline: Wanted Saudi reportedly admitted Hizbollah ties.

text.p: A Saudi dissident arrested by Canada has admitted to having been a member of the Saudi Hizbollah group linked by Canadian intelligence to last June's bombing in Saudi Arabia that killed 19 U.S. airmen, the Toronto Star reported on Saturday.
The newspaper said the Shiite Muslim dissident, Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh, 28, made the admission in a prison interview on Friday with the Star.

Canada arrested Sayegh in Ottawa last month and charged him with having been a driver involved in the massive truck bomb last June 25 in eastern Saudi Arabia. It said it had reasonable grounds to believe he was a member of Saudi Hizbollah, which it said orchestrated the bombing.
"I was with them in the past and had some disagreement with them and quit," the Star quoted Sayegh as saying of the group.
He again denied having participated in the bombing but appeared to have changed his line on where he was on June 25.

Sayegh, clean-cut and quiet-spoken, had told reporters from Reuters and a few other media organizations on March 24 that he had been in self-imposed exile in Syria at the time, and denied links with any terrorist organizations.
But the Star quoted him as saying he was with his Saudi wife in Qom, the main Shiite learning center in Iran, on the day of the bombing and learned about it from a broadcast on Iranian television.
"I am innocent and I am not scared of anything," it quoted him as saying through an interpereter.

He said he had been scared to admit, when he arrived in Ottawa last August, that he had been to Iran since he was afraid it would affect his application to be a refugee from persecution by the Saudi government, ruled by Sunni Muslims.
"Now is the time to tell the truth," he was quoted as saying.

The Canadian intelligence service, in papers released at the Canadian Federal Court last month, asserted that Hizbollah -- which means Party of Allah or Party of God -- had an "infrastructure in Canada that can assist and support terrorists seeking a safe haven in North America."
It said Hizbollah members in Canada receive and comply with direction from the Hizbollah leadership in Lebanon -- where it has been linked to kidnappings and possible bombings.
The papers referred to a 1994 Federal Court case in which Mohammad Hussein al-Husseini admitted to being a member of Hizbollah and to that group operating in Canada.
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation said last month it wanted to question Sayegh on the bombing, and the Star said an FBI team was now in Canada hoping to interview him.
Sayegh's refugee papers say he flew to Ottawa on Aug. 15-16 from Kuwait, transiting via Italy and the United States.

Admitting being a member of what Canada terms a terrorist organization would normally be enough to deport Sayegh. But it was not clear whether this would be to Saudi Arabia, the United States or another destination if this were to happen.
He is scheduled to appear before the Federal Court in Ottawa on April 28.
